title: Harmonic Analysis
text: Fourier series and transforms describe functions through oscillatory bases. Spherical harmonics extend this construction to the sphere. The chapters develop the shared function-space theory, coefficients, convergence, and spectral identities used in numerical PDEs, fluid dynamics, and operator learning.

title: 7  Fourier analysis
text:
7.1 Periodic modes and coefficient recovery
Why does decomposing a field into oscillations simplify differential equations? Periodic exponentials turn differentiation into multiplication, while the whole-line limit replaces a discrete mode sum by a continuous wavenumber integral. We derive these conventions first and then distinguish an exact discrete transform from adequate physical sampling.
Fourier modes diagonalize translation-invariant differentiation on a periodic domain. Orthogonality determines the coefficients and normalization. Sources: (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 14.1–14.4).

title: 7  Fourier analysis
text:
Definition M7.1 - Periodic coordinate and Fourier coefficients
Let \(x\) be a length coordinate with period \(d>0\): values at \(x\) and \(x+d\) are identified. The integer mode index is \(n\in\mathbb Z\) and angular wavenumber is \(k_n=2\pi n/d\). Define \(c_n\) by
\[
f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}c_ne^{ik_nx},
\qquad c_n=\frac1d\int_0^df(x)e^{-ik_nx}dx,
\qquad \frac1d\int_0^de^{i(k_n-k_m)x}dx=\delta_{nm}.
\tag{M7.1}
\]


Result M7.2 - Periodic orthogonality and coefficient selection
The exponentials \(e^{ik_nx}\), \(k_n=2\pi n/d\), are orthonormal under \(dx/d\). For an expansion whose convergence permits integration term by term, its coefficients are those in (M7.1).


Proof of Result M7.2
For \(n\ne m\), integrate the exponential and use \(e^{2\pi i(n-m)}=1\) to obtain zero. For \(n=m\), the integrand is one. Multiplying the expansion by \(e^{-ik_mx}\) and integrating therefore selects \(c_m\). With normalized measure \(dx/d\), these exponentials are orthonormal and \(c_n\) has the units of \(f\). Under \(dx\), the normalized basis would instead be \(d^{-1/2}e^{ik_nx}\). \(\square\)


Result M7.3 - Fourier completeness, Parseval, and derivatives
The periodic exponentials form a complete orthonormal system in \(L^2([0,d],dx/d)\). Parseval holds for every such field; if \(f\) is continuously differentiable with matching periodic values, its derivative coefficients satisfy
\[
\frac1d\int_0^d|f|^2dx=\sum_n|c_n|^2,
\qquad \widehat{\partial_xf}_n=ik_nc_n.
\tag{M7.2}
\]


Proof of Result M7.3
Completeness is the Fourier completeness theorem (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 14.1–14.4). Apply the abstract Parseval identity from function spaces. For differentiation, integrate \(d^{-1}\int_0^df\prime e^{-ik_nx}dx\) by parts; periodicity removes the endpoint term and leaves \(ik_nc_n\). \(\square\)


Remark M7.4 - Reality and the mean
For a real field \(c_{-n}=\overline{c_n}\); the pair \(n,-n\) is \(2\operatorname{Re}(c_ne^{ik_nx})\). The zero mode \(c_0\) is the spatial mean. Taking real and imaginary parts gives the equivalent sine-cosine series.


Example M7.5 - A sine-cosine pair and its mean square
For \(f=A\cos(k_px)+B\sin(k_px)\), with positive integer \(p\) and real amplitudes \(A,B\), the only nonzero coefficients are \(c_p=(A-iB)/2\) and \(c_{-p}=(A+iB)/2\). Equation (M7.2) gives mean square \((A^2+B^2)/2\), checking both the conjugation and the factor two.


Exercise M7.1 - A phase-rotated coefficient
Application. For \(f(x)=\cos(x-\alpha)\) on a \(2\pi\) interval, find \(c_1,c_{-1}\) and the mean square.

title: 7  Fourier analysis
text:
7.2 Convergence, smoothness, and Gibbs oscillations
Smoothness controls coefficient decay, but a truncated expansion near a jump retains an overshoot. Spectral accuracy requires appropriate regularity and periodic matching. Sources: (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 5.5, 14.4–14.5).

Result M7.6 - Smooth periodic data have decaying coefficients
Let \(p\ge1\) be an integer and \(f\in C^p([0,d])\), with matching periodic derivatives through order \(p-1\). Then, for \(n\ne0\),
\[
c_n=\frac{\widehat{f^{(p)}}_n}{(ik_n)^p},
\qquad |c_n|\le\frac{1}{d|k_n|^p}\int_0^d|f^{(p)}(x)|dx.
\tag{M7.3}
\]


Proof of Result M7.6
Integrate the coefficient integral by parts \(p\) times. Matching periodic traces through order \(p-1\) remove every endpoint term. Divide by \((ik_n)^p\) and bound the remaining integral by its absolute integral to obtain (M7.3). \(\square\)


Counterexample M7.7 - Smooth inside an interval is not smooth periodically
The endpoint requirements remove boundary terms. Smoothness on the open interval alone is insufficient: the periodic extension of \(f(x)=x\) on \((-\pi,\pi)\) has a jump at the identified endpoints and coefficients of order \(1/|n|\).


Result M7.8 - Pointwise convergence and Gibbs behavior (quoted)
For a piecewise smooth periodic \(f\), its Fourier sum at a jump tends to the midpoint of its one-sided limits. Partial sums overshoot near a jump; increasing the cutoff narrows this region without making its limiting relative height vanish (Gibbs phenomenon). (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 14.4–14.5).


Example M7.9 - A discontinuous square wave
For the square wave \(f(x)=1\) on \((0,\pi)\) and \(f(x)=-1\) on \((-\pi,0)\),
\[
b_n=\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi\sin(nx)dx
=\frac{2[1-(-1)^n]}{\pi n},
\qquad f(x)\sim\frac4\pi\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{\sin((2j+1)x)}{2j+1}.
\tag{M7.4}
\]
Here \(\sim\) denotes the Fourier representation with the convergence just specified, rather than equality at every assigned point value. Damping high modes can suppress ringing but changes the approximated function. Parseval still permits good mean-square approximation when a uniform approximation near a jump is impossible.


Exercise M7.2 - Find the missing endpoint hypothesis
Counterexample. A polynomial is smooth on \([0,d]\). Does that alone guarantee rapid decay of its periodic Fourier coefficients? Give a counterexample.

title: 7  Fourier analysis
section: 7.3 The Fourier transform and its normalization
text:
7.3 The Fourier transform and its normalization
On the whole line, wavenumber becomes continuous. The transform turns constant-coefficient differentiation into multiplication. Sources: (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 15.1–15.4).

Definition M7.10 - Angular-wavenumber Fourier pair
For \(f\in L^1(\mathbb R)\) define the angular-wavenumber transform, with the following sign convention:
\[
\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-ikx}dx,
\qquad f(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}\widehat f(k)e^{ikx}dk.
\tag{M7.5}
\]


Result M7.11 - Fourier inversion and its sense of convergence (quoted)
The inverse formula holds, for example, for smooth rapidly decaying functions. More generally, integrability of both \(f\) and \(\widehat f\) gives the continuous representative almost everywhere; \(L^2\) inversion is in norm and uses the Plancherel extension, not necessarily an absolutely convergent integral. A rapidly decaying smooth function and all its derivatives decay faster than every inverse power of \(|x|\). (Arfken and Weber 2005, sec. 15.3).


Example M7.12 - The continuum limit fixes the inverse factor
To see the factor \(1/(2\pi)\), put the periodic problem on \([-d/2,d/2]\) and define \(\Delta k=2\pi/d\). Then \(c_n=d^{-1}\int f(x)e^{-ik_nx}dx\approx\widehat f(k_n)\Delta k/(2\pi)\). As \(d\to\infty\), the Fourier sum becomes the integral in (M7.5), under suitable decay assumptions. AW often uses a symmetric \(1/\sqrt{2\pi}\) normalization and the opposite forward sign; coefficients must be converted before comparison.


Result M7.13 - Differentiation, translation, and Plancherel
For smooth rapidly decaying \(f\), with \(\mathcal F\) denoting (M7.5) and \(a\) a spatial shift,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{f'}(k)&=ik\widehat f(k),\qquad \widehat{f''}(k)=-k^2\widehat f(k),\\
\mathcal F[f(x-a)](k)&=e^{-ika}\widehat f(k),\\
\int_{\mathbb R}|f|^2dx&=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}|\widehat f|^2dk.
\end{aligned}
\tag{M7.6}
\]
The last identity extends to \(L^2\) by the Plancherel theorem.


Proof of Result M7.13
Integration by parts removes the boundary term for \(f\prime\) and produces \(ik\); repeat once for \(f\prime\prime\). For a shift set \(y=x-a\) in the defining integral. The final identity is the Fourier Parseval theorem under the normalization in (M7.5) (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 15.3–15.4). \(\square\)


Remark M7.14 - Dimensions and cyclic frequency
The symbol \(\mathcal F\) denotes the transform in (M7.5), and \(a\) is a spatial shift. With \([x]=\mathrm m\) and \([f]=U\), \([k]=\mathrm m^{-1}\) and \([\widehat f]=U\,\mathrm m\). A transform with cyclic frequency \(\xi=k/(2\pi)\) instead has \(e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\) and no inverse \(1/(2\pi)\) prefactor. The variable and the measure change together.


Exercise M7.3 - Track transform units
Application. If \([f]=\mathrm K\) and \([x]=\mathrm m\), what are the units of \(\widehat f(k)\), \(dk\), and the inverse integral?

title: 7  Fourier analysis
text:
7.4 Convolution and the heat kernel
Convolution sums responses to shifted sources. Fourier multiplication provides both its algebraic representation and a direct diffusion solution. Sources: (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 9.8, 15.4–15.5).

Definition M7.15 - Whole-line convolution
For integrable \(f,g\), define convolution by \((f*g)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(y)g(x-y)dy\).


Result M7.16 - Convolution becomes multiplication
If \(f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R)\), their convolution has transform
\[
\widehat{f*g}(k)
=\int\!\int f(y)g(z)e^{-ik(y+z)}dy\,dz
=\widehat f(k)\widehat g(k).
\tag{M7.7}
\]


Proof of Result M7.16
In the double integral set \(z=x-y\). Absolute integrability of \(f(y)g(z)\) permits interchange of the integrals; the exponential factors into \(e^{-iky}e^{-ikz}\), leaving the product in (M7.7). \(\square\)


Remark M7.17 - Products couple wavenumbers
Absolute integrability justifies changing the integration order. A product instead becomes \(\widehat{fg}(k)=(2\pi)^{-1}(\widehat f*\widehat g)(k)\), when the functions have enough integrability. Thus nonlinear multiplication couples frequencies rather than acting diagonally.


Model M7.18 - Diffusion on the whole line
Take \(u_t=\kappa u_{xx}\), \(\kappa>0\), on \(\mathbb R\), with smooth rapidly decaying initial data \(u_0\). We seek the field at \(t>0\).


Result M7.19 - Heat evolution is Gaussian smoothing
In this model the Fourier amplitudes and physical solution are
\[
\widehat u(k,t)=e^{-\kappa k^2t}\widehat u_0(k),
\qquad u(x,t)=(G_t*u_0)(x),
\qquad G_t(x)=\frac{e^{-x^2/(4\kappa t)}}{\sqrt{4\pi\kappa t}},\quad t>0.
\tag{M7.8}
\]


Proof of Result M7.19
For \(u_t=\kappa u_{xx}\) on \(\mathbb R\), transforming only in \(x\) gives \(\partial_t\widehat u=-\kappa k^2\widehat u\). Solve this scalar ODE and invert:
To verify the inverse Gaussian, let \(I(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-ak^2}e^{ikx}dk\) for \(a>0\). Integrating \(\partial_k(e^{-ak^2})\) by parts gives \(I'=-xI/(2a)\), hence \(I(x)=I(0)e^{-x^2/(4a)}\). Squaring \(I(0)\) and using polar coordinates gives \(I(0)^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-a(k^2+s^2)}dkds=\pi/a\). With \(a=\kappa t\), dividing by \(2\pi\) gives (M7.8). The kernel integrates to one and has units of inverse length, preserving total mass for integrable initial data. Its width grows as \(\sqrt{\kappa t}\). \(\square\)


Exercise M7.4 - Read a diffusive length
Application. In (M7.8), at what \(|x|\) has the Gaussian exponent reached \(-1\)? How does that distance change when time is multiplied by four?

title: 7  Fourier analysis
text:
7.5 The discrete transform and aliasing
A DFT exactly represents a finite vector. Its coefficients equal continuous Fourier coefficients only with adequate sampling assumptions. Sources: (Arfken and Weber 2005, sec. 14.6).

Definition M7.20 - Normalized DFT and synthesis
For \(N\) samples \(f_j=f(jd/N)\), \(j=0,\ldots,N-1\), use normalized discrete coefficients
\[
\widetilde c_n=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}f_je^{-2\pi inj/N},
\qquad f_j=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\widetilde c_ne^{2\pi inj/N}.
\tag{M7.9}
\]


Result M7.21 - Discrete orthogonality and finite inversion
For any complex vector of length \(N\), the DFT pair (M7.9) is an exact inverse pair. Its frequencies are equivalent modulo \(N\).


Proof of Result M7.21
The discrete orthogonality sum \(N^{-1}\sum_j e^{2\pi i(n-m)j/N}\) is one when \(n-m\) is a multiple of \(N\) and zero otherwise, by the geometric-series formula. Therefore mode indices are defined modulo \(N\); indices above half the sample count represent negative wavenumbers. For even \(N\), the Nyquist index \(N/2\) coincides with its negative, so it is a special endpoint and cannot represent two independent traveling phases. \(\square\)


Result M7.22 - Aliasing and discrete Parseval
Let \(f\) be a continuous periodic function with absolutely summable Fourier coefficients, \(\sum_n|c_n|<\infty\). Sampling this continuous representative on \(N\) equally spaced nodes gives the first identity below. The second holds for every finite sample vector.
\[
\widetilde c_n=\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}c_{n+rN},
\qquad \frac1N\sum_j|f_j|^2=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|\widetilde c_n|^2.
\tag{M7.10}
\]


Proof of Result M7.22
Insert the absolutely convergent Fourier series into the DFT sum and interchange the finite sample sum with the series. Discrete orthogonality retains exactly indices \(n+rN\). For Parseval insert the finite synthesis into \(N^{-1}\sum_jf_j\overline f_j\); all unequal discrete modes cancel. \(\square\)


Example M7.23 - An exact round trip can conceal an aliased wave
The first formula is aliasing: unresolved modes contaminate the same sampled coefficient. A field bandlimited to \(|n|\le K\) (all higher coefficients zero) is recovered uniquely if \(N\ge2K+1\). With \(N=8\), mode \(6\) samples exactly as mode \(-2\). A correct forward-inverse round trip cannot detect that loss of continuous information. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes the same DFT in \(O(N\log N)\) work; it is an algorithm, not a different transform. Discrete convolution is circular (indices wrap modulo \(N\)); linear convolution requires padding.


Exercise M7.5 - Find the aliased index
Application. On \(N=10\) equally spaced points, which signed mode in \([-5,4]\) has the same samples as mode \(7\)?

title: 7  Fourier analysis
text:
7.6 Chapter summary
Fourier coefficients follow from periodic orthogonality. Differentiation multiplies by \(ik\); the Laplacian multiplies by \(-k^2\). Parseval equates mean square or integrated square with coefficient power under the stated normalization. Endpoint regularity controls coefficient decay. The whole-line transform has a continuous wavenumber and a paired inverse factor. Convolution becomes multiplication; diffusion becomes Gaussian smoothing. A DFT is exact for samples, while aliasing limits its interpretation as continuous analysis.

Exercise M7.6 - Connect the chapter results
Synthesis. Find the nonzero Fourier coefficients and mean square of \(3\cos(2x)\) on a \(2\pi\) interval. Explain why a round trip of an undersampled wave can be exact. Derive the decay rate of the \(n\)th periodic diffusion mode.





Arfken, George B., and Hans J. Weber. 2005. Mathematical Methods for Physicists. 6th ed. Elsevier Academic Press.

title: 8  Legendre polynomials and spherical harmonics
text:
8.1 Angular separation and Legendre’s equation
What replaces periodic plane waves on a sphere? Separation in longitude produces integer orders, while regularity at the poles selects discrete degrees. We use that eigenproblem to fix the Legendre normalization, construct spherical harmonics, and distinguish scalar profiles from tangent vector fields.
Spherical harmonics are the globally regular eigenfunctions of the spherical Laplacian. Longitude periodicity and pole regularity quantize their two indices. Sources: (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 9.3-9.5, 12.1-12.6).

title: 8  Legendre polynomials and spherical harmonics
text:
Assumption M8.1 - A globally regular angular eigenfunction
Seek \(\Delta_\Omega Y=-\Lambda Y\) on the unit sphere, where \(\Lambda\) is dimensionless and \(Y(\theta,\lambda)=\Theta(\theta)\Phi(\lambda)\).


Result M8.2 - Angular separation produces an associated Legendre equation
For a separated angular eigenfunction with \(2\pi\)-periodic longitude factor, the order \(m\) is an integer, and its latitude factor obeys
\[
\frac{d}{d\mu}\left[(1-\mu^2)\frac{d\Theta}{d\mu}\right]
+\left[\Lambda-\frac{m^2}{1-\mu^2}\right]\Theta=0.
\tag{M8.1}
\]


Proof of Result M8.2
Insert \(Y=\Theta(\theta)\Phi(\lambda)\) into (M3.5), multiply by \(\sin^2\theta\), and separate the two variable dependences. The longitude equation is \(\Phi\prime\prime+m^2\Phi=0\), whose single-valued periodic solutions require integer \(m\). Choose \(\Phi=e^{im\lambda}\) and set \(\mu=\cos\theta\). \(\square\)


Result M8.3 - Power-series recurrence at order zero
For \(m=0\) and a power-series solution \(\Theta=\sum_{j\ge0}a_j\mu^j\) near zero,
\[
a_{j+2}=\frac{j(j+1)-\Lambda}{(j+2)(j+1)}a_j.
\tag{M8.2}
\]


Proof of Result M8.3
The coefficient of \(\mu^j\) in \((1-\mu^2)\Theta\prime\prime-2\mu\Theta\prime+\Lambda\Theta\) is \((j+2)(j+1)a_{j+2}+[\Lambda-j(j+1)]a_j\). Set it to zero. \(\square\)


Result M8.4 - Regular degrees and polynomial solutions (quoted)
If \(\Lambda=\ell(\ell+1)\) for \(\ell\in\mathbb N_0\), one parity branch terminates at degree \(\ell\). Its normalization \(P_\ell(1)=1\) defines the Legendre polynomial \(P_\ell\). The other independent solution is singular at an endpoint. The global regularity theorem for (M8.1) selects these discrete eigenvalues; the recurrence exhibits the regular polynomial solutions but is not by itself a proof that all other \(\Lambda\) fail both endpoint conditions. For integer \(m\ne0\), admissible degrees satisfy \(\ell\ge|m|\). (Arfken and Weber 2005, sec. 9.5 and 12.5-12.6).


Remark M8.5 - Pole conditions are endpoint regularity
For \(m=0\) the Legendre equation has singular Sturm-Liouville endpoints because \(p=1-\mu^2\) vanishes at \(\pm1\). The boundary condition is regularity of the scalar on the sphere, rather than arbitrary Dirichlet data at coordinate poles.


Exercise M8.1 - Terminate a recurrence
Application. At \(m=0\) and \(\Lambda=2\), use (M8.2) to obtain the odd regular polynomial with \(P(1)=1\).

title: 8  Legendre polynomials and spherical harmonics
text:
8.2 Polynomial normalization and associated functions
Explicit normalization and phase conventions make coefficients comparable. Associated Legendre functions supply the latitude dependence for nonzero longitude order. Sources: (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 12.2–12.5).

Result M8.6 - Rodrigues representation and Legendre orthogonality
For the regular degree-\(\ell\) solution normalized by \(P_\ell(1)=1\), Rodrigues’ representation and orthogonality are
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_\ell(\mu)&=\frac1{2^\ell\ell!}\frac{d^\ell}{d\mu^\ell}(\mu^2-1)^\ell,\\
P_0&=1,\quad P_1=\mu,\quad P_2=\tfrac12(3\mu^2-1),\\
\int_{-1}^1P_\ell(\mu)P_j(\mu)d\mu&=\frac2{2\ell+1}\delta_{\ell j}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{M8.3}
\]
Rodrigues’ representation is quoted from AW, Section 12.4; the norm and orthogonality can be derived from it.


Proof of Result M8.6
Orthogonality for different degrees follows by multiplying their differential equations, subtracting, and integrating; the boundary factor \(1-\mu^2\) makes the regular polynomial boundary terms zero. The norm can also be derived from Rodrigues. The leading coefficient of \(P_\ell\) is \(a_\ell=(2\ell)!/[2^\ell(\ell!)^2]\). Since \(P_\ell-a_\ell\mu^\ell\) has lower degree, orthogonality gives \(\int P_\ell^2=a_\ell\int P_\ell\mu^\ell\). Define \(I_\ell=\int_{-1}^1(1-\mu^2)^\ell d\mu\). Integrating Rodrigues by parts \(\ell\) times gives \(\int P_\ell\mu^\ell=2^{-\ell}I_\ell\): all endpoint terms vanish and \(d^\ell\mu^\ell/d\mu^\ell=\ell!\).
For \(\ell\ge1\), integrate the derivative of \(\mu(1-\mu^2)^\ell\) over \([-1,1]\) to get \(0=I_\ell-2\ell(I_{\ell-1}-I_\ell)\). Thus \(I_\ell=2\ell I_{\ell-1}/(2\ell+1)\) with \(I_0=2\). Iterating gives \(I_\ell=2^{2\ell+1}(\ell!)^2/(2\ell+1)!\), and the norm is \(a_\ell2^{-\ell}I_\ell=2/(2\ell+1)\). \(\square\)


Definition M8.7 - Associated functions and the Condon-Shortley phase
For integer \(0\le m\le\ell\), choose the Condon-Shortley phase by defining
\[
P_\ell^m(\mu)=(-1)^m(1-\mu^2)^{m/2}\frac{d^mP_\ell}{d\mu^m},
\qquad
\int_{-1}^1(P_\ell^m)^2d\mu
=\frac2{2\ell+1}\frac{(\ell+m)!}{(\ell-m)!}.
\tag{M8.4}
\]
The second identity is a quoted normalization result (Arfken and Weber 2005, sec. 12.5).


Remark M8.8 - Pole factors and the quoted associated norm
Differentiating Legendre’s equation \(m\) times and multiplying by \((1-\mu^2)^{m/2}\) gives (M8.1). The associated-function norm in (M8.4) is quoted from AW, Section 12.5; its repeated-integration proof is not reproduced here. The factor \((1-\mu^2)^{m/2}=\sin^m\theta\) enforces the required vanishing of a regular scalar’s nonzero longitude order at the poles. Odd-\(m\) associated functions are not polynomials in \(\mu\).


Result M8.9 - Degree recurrence (quoted)
A stable degree recurrence follows from Rodrigues or the generating function: \((\ell+1)P_{\ell+1}=(2\ell+1)\mu P_\ell-\ell P_{\ell-1}\). It constructs all degrees from \(P_0,P_1\); high-degree numerical algorithms still need controlled normalization to avoid overflow. (Arfken and Weber 2005, sec. 12.2).


Exercise M8.2 - Generate the next degree
Application. Use the degree recurrence and \(P_1=\mu\), \(P_2=(3\mu^2-1)/2\) to obtain \(P_3\).

title: 8  Legendre polynomials and spherical harmonics
text:
8.3 Spherical harmonic expansion and Parseval
The spherical harmonic transform is longitude Fourier analysis coupled to weighted latitude analysis. Degree measures total angular scale; order measures longitude variation. Sources: (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 12.5–12.6).

Definition M8.10 - Normalized complex spherical harmonics
For \(m\ge0\), define
\[
Y_\ell^m(\theta,\lambda)=N_{\ell m}P_\ell^m(\cos\theta)e^{im\lambda},
\qquad N_{\ell m}=\left[\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}\frac{(\ell-m)!}{(\ell+m)!}\right]^{1/2},
\qquad Y_\ell^{-m}=(-1)^m\overline{Y_\ell^m}.
\tag{M8.5}
\]
Degree \(\ell\) is nonnegative, and order satisfies \(-\ell\le m\le\ell\).


Result M8.11 - Angular orthonormality and the physical eigenvalue
For the convention (M8.5),
\[
\int_{S^2}Y_\ell^m\overline{Y_j^n}d\Omega=\delta_{\ell j}\delta_{mn},
\qquad \Delta_sY_\ell^m=-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{R^2}Y_\ell^m.
\tag{M8.6}
\]


Proof of Result M8.11
Longitude integration removes unequal orders. For equal nonnegative order \(m\) but unequal degrees \(\ell,j\), multiply the two associated Legendre equations by the other function, subtract, and integrate. The \(m^2/(1-\mu^2)\) terms cancel, giving
\[
[\ell(\ell+1)-j(j+1)]\int_{-1}^1 P_\ell^mP_j^m\,d\mu
=\left[(1-\mu^2)\left(P_\ell^m(P_j^m)\prime-(P_\ell^m)\prime P_j^m\right)\right]_{-1}^1=0.
\]
Regularity makes the endpoint bracket zero: for \(m=0\) the polynomial factors are finite, and for \(m>0\) the pole factors in (M8.4) make the product vanish. Distinct degrees have different \(\ell(\ell+1)\), proving the cross integral is zero. For equal degrees use (M8.4), whose factorials cancel \(N_{\ell m}^2\). The eigenvalue follows by substituting the separated equations into \(\Delta_s=R^{-2}\Delta_\Omega\). Negative orders follow by conjugation. \(\square\)


Remark M8.12 - The measure belongs to the normalization
The symbol \(S^2\) denotes the unit sphere; these angular functions are also evaluated on \(S_R^2\). They are normalized under \(d\Omega\), not physical area \(dA\). In particular \(Y_0^0=1/\sqrt{4\pi}\) and \(Y_1^0=\sqrt{3/(4\pi)}\cos\theta\).


Result M8.13 - Spherical harmonic expansion and Parseval
The harmonics form a complete orthonormal system in \(L^2(S^2,d\Omega)\). For any \(f\) in that space,
\[
\begin{aligned}
f&=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}f_\ell^mY_\ell^m,
& f_\ell^m&=\int_{S^2}f\overline{Y_\ell^m}d\Omega,\\
\int_{S^2}|f|^2d\Omega&=\sum_{\ell,m}|f_\ell^m|^2,
& \langle f\rangle_A&=f_0^0/\sqrt{4\pi}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{M8.7}
\]
The expansion converges in norm; completeness is quoted from AW, Section 12.6. Parseval follows from function spaces.


Proof of Result M8.13
The completeness assertion is the cited spherical harmonic theorem. Apply the Hilbert-space projection and Parseval results of function spaces with the double index \((\ell,m)\) to obtain the norm limit and squared-coefficient sum. Only the constant harmonic has nonzero area integral, so \(\langle f\rangle_A=f_0^0/\sqrt{4\pi}\). \(\square\)


Remark M8.14 - Real fields and a degree cutoff
The expansion converges in \(L^2\); smooth fields admit stronger convergence. Real \(f\) obeys \(f_\ell^{-m}=(-1)^m\overline{f_\ell^m}\). A cutoff \(0\le\ell\le L\) retains \((L+1)^2\) basis functions, or the same number of independent real coefficients for a real field. The physical inverse length is approximately \(\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}/R\); degree zero is the mean, not a finite wavelength.


Example M8.15 - Expanding squared sine of latitude
For \(f=\mu^2\), equation (M8.3) gives \(\mu^2=P_0/3+2P_2/3\). Hence \(f_0^0=\sqrt{4\pi}/3\), \(f_2^0=(2/3)\sqrt{4\pi/5}\), and all other coefficients vanish. The area mean is \(1/3\). Parseval gives \(\int\mu^4d\Omega=4\pi/5\), agreeing with direct integration.


Exercise M8.3 - Recover a constant mode
Application. For \(f(\mathbf n)=C\), find \(f_0^0\) and verify the area mean using (M8.7).

section: 8.4 Zonal means, tangent vectors, and isotropy
text:
8.4 Zonal means, tangent vectors, and isotropy
Longitude averaging keeps only order zero. Tangent vectors need geometric basis functions, while rotationally invariant scalar filters must act identically on all orders of a degree. Sources: (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 12.6, 12.8, 12.11).

Definition M8.16 - Zonal mean and normalized latitude basis
The zonal mean is \(\overline f(\mu)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}f(\mu,\lambda)d\lambda\). Because the average of \(e^{im\lambda}\) is zero for \(m\ne0\), only \(m=0\) survives. For a profile use \(b_\ell(\mu)=\sqrt{2\ell+1}P_\ell(\mu)\), orthonormal under \(d\mu/2\). Then \(\overline f=\sum_\ell a_\ell b_\ell\) with \(a_\ell=\frac12\int_{-1}^1\overline f b_\ell d\mu\). A scalar profile and an eastward velocity component have different pole regularity: an arbitrary scalar Legendre expansion of speed does not by itself define a smooth tangent vector field.


Definition M8.17 - Tangent gradient and rotated-gradient harmonics
For \(\ell\ge1\), dimensionless tangent vector harmonics are
\[
\mathbf E_\ell^m=\frac{R\nabla_sY_\ell^m}{\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}},
\qquad
\mathbf B_\ell^m=\mathbf e_r\times\mathbf E_\ell^m.
\tag{M8.8}
\]


Result M8.18 - Tangent harmonic normalization and differential type
For each \(\ell\ge1\) and \(|m|\le\ell\), the tangent harmonics (M8.8) both have unit norm under \(d\Omega\). The gradient family is surface-curl-free; the rotated-gradient family is divergence-free. The convention here is the tangent gradient/rotated-gradient convention, whereas AW also uses coupled vector harmonics with radial components.


Proof of Result M8.18
Integration by parts gives \(\int R^2|\nabla_sY_\ell^m|^2d\Omega=-R^2\int\overline{Y_\ell^m}\Delta_sY_\ell^m d\Omega=\ell(\ell+1)\). Divide by the squared normalizing factor in (M8.8). Rotation by \(\mathbf e_r\times\) preserves tangent length, so the rotated family has the same norm. The curl of a gradient and the divergence of its rotated gradient vanish by cancellation of mixed derivatives in (M3.4). \(\square\)


Definition M8.19 - A harmonic tangent field
A smooth tangent field with zero surface divergence and zero radial curl is called a harmonic tangent field.


Result M8.20 - Smooth tangent decomposition on the sphere
Every smooth tangent field on the whole sphere can be written \(\mathbf v=\nabla_s\chi+\mathbf e_r\times\nabla_s\psi\), with scalar potentials unique up to constants. A smooth divergence-free field therefore has a streamfunction.


Proof of Result M8.20
For a smooth tangent field \(\mathbf v\), let \(\delta=\nabla_s\cdot\mathbf v\) and \(\zeta=(\nabla\times\mathbf v)\cdot\mathbf e_r\). Both have zero area integral by the surface divergence and Stokes identities. Scalar harmonic inversion therefore supplies zero-mean potentials \(\chi,\psi\) with \(\Delta_s\chi=\delta\) and \(\Delta_s\psi=\zeta\), by dividing each degree-\(\ell\ge1\) coefficient by \(-\ell(\ell+1)/R^2\). Then \(\mathbf w=\mathbf v-\nabla_s\chi-\mathbf e_r\times\nabla_s\psi\) has zero divergence and radial curl. Such a field is called a harmonic tangent field.
The sphere is simply connected: every closed loop can be continuously shrunk to a point. Stokes’ theorem therefore makes the integral of a curl-free smooth tangent field around every loop zero. Its line integral from a reference point is path-independent and defines a scalar \(h\) with \(\mathbf w=\nabla_sh\) (the potential-field argument of AW, Section 1.13). Since \(\Delta_sh=0\), (M3.8) gives \(\int|\nabla_sh|^2dA=0\), hence \(\mathbf w=0\). This proves the smooth decomposition \(\mathbf v=\nabla_s\chi+\mathbf e_r\times\nabla_s\psi\). In particular, a divergence-free smooth field has the streamfunction representation. Expanding these potentials gives the \(\mathbf E/\mathbf B\) modes; the construction here only needs smooth fields. A velocity generated from a streamfunction uses the latter family; treating its coordinate components as unrelated scalars does not encode that constraint. \(\square\)


Result M8.21 - Spherical addition theorem (quoted)
For unit vectors \(\mathbf n,\mathbf n'\) separated by angle \(\gamma\), with \(\cos\gamma=\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n'\), the addition theorem is
\[
P_\ell(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n')
=\frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}Y_\ell^m(\mathbf n)\overline{Y_\ell^m(\mathbf n')}.
\tag{M8.9}
\]
This theorem uses the normalization (M8.5) (Arfken and Weber 2005, sec. 12.8).


Remark M8.22 - Why all orders of a degree belong together
This theorem is quoted from AW, Section 12.8. It shows why an isotropic kernel, depending only on angular separation, multiplies every order at fixed degree by the same scalar. integral and learned operators derives the multiplier. Keeping all orders through a degree gives a rotation-invariant subspace (triangular truncation). Selecting unrelated orders can break that property.


Exercise M8.4 - Apply zonal averaging
Application. What is the zonal mean of \(Y_\ell^m\) when \(m\ne0\)? What happens for \(m=0\)?

9.1 Projection and the method of weighted residuals
When does a finite spectral calculation approximate the continuum problem it is intended to solve? Choosing a finite basis, integrating its coefficients, and advancing them in time are separate decisions. We derive sufficient sampling bounds for scalar products and use modal amplification to check time integration.
A spectral method approximates a field in a finite basis and imposes equations on its coefficients. Spatial truncation and time integration introduce different errors. Sources: (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 10.4, 12.3, 14.6, 17.8); numerical bounds below are derived for the stated finite spaces.

title: 9  Spectral discretization, quadrature, and stability
text:
Definition M9.1 - Finite expansion and Galerkin residual
For an evolution equation \(u_t=\mathcal Lu+\mathcal N(u)+f\), let \(\mathcal L\) be a linear spatial operator, \(\mathcal N\) a nonlinear term, and \(f\) forcing. Choose orthonormal basis functions \(e_1,\ldots,e_K\) satisfying the spatial conditions, and approximate \(u_K=\sum_{j=1}^Ka_j(t)e_j\). The residual is \(r_K=\partial_tu_K-\mathcal Lu_K-\mathcal N(u_K)-f\).


Result M9.2 - Galerkin coefficient equations
For an orthonormal basis satisfying the spatial conditions and enough regularity to form the displayed inner products, requiring \(\langle r_K,e_i\rangle=0\) gives
\[
a_i'=\sum_jL_{ij}a_j+\langle\mathcal N(u_K),e_i\rangle+f_i,
\quad L_{ij}=\langle\mathcal Le_j,e_i\rangle,
\quad f_i=\langle f,e_i\rangle.
\tag{M9.1}
\]


Proof of Result M9.2
Insert \(u_K=\sum_ja_je_j\) into the residual. Orthonormality makes \(\langle\partial_tu_K,e_i\rangle=a_i\prime\). Linearity of \(\mathcal L\) gives the matrix term, and moving the other terms to the right yields (M9.1). \(\square\)


Definition M9.3 - Mass matrix, collocation, and pseudospectral evaluation
If \(\mathcal Le_j=\lambda_je_j\), \(L_{ij}=\lambda_j\delta_{ij}\). A nonorthonormal basis instead gives a mass matrix \(M_{ij}=\langle e_j,e_i\rangle\) multiplying \(a_j'\). Collocation requires the PDE residual to vanish at selected nodes. A pseudospectral method evaluates products at grid points and transforms them back; with sufficiently accurate quadrature this reproduces Galerkin projection for those products.


Remark M9.4 - Three independent approximation choices
Three separate approximations are present: truncating the function space, approximating its integrals, and integrating its coefficient ODEs in time. Increasing the grid alone does not increase the retained degree; decreasing the time step does not remove spatial aliasing.


Exercise M9.1 - Diagonalize one linear term
Application. If \(\mathcal Le_j=-j^2e_j\) and forcing and nonlinearity vanish, derive the Galerkin ODE and its exact solution for \(a_j(0)=A_j\).

section: 9.2 Gauss-Legendre quadrature and a spherical grid
text:
9.2 Gauss-Legendre quadrature and a spherical grid
Gaussian quadrature integrates polynomials up to degree \(2n-1\) using \(n\) carefully chosen latitude nodes. It accounts for spherical area through \(\mu=\sin\varphi\). Sources: Legendre orthogonality (Arfken and Weber 2005, sec. 12.3); explicit quadrature rule (NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, n.d.).

Definition M9.5 - Gaussian nodes and polynomial degree
For \(n\ge1\), let \(\mu_i\) be the distinct roots of \(P_n\) in \((-1,1)\). The notation \(\deg p\) means the degree of polynomial \(p\).


Result M9.6 - Gauss-Legendre weights and exactness
The weights below integrate every polynomial of degree at most \(2n-1\) exactly:
\[
\int_{-1}^1p(\mu)d\mu=\sum_{i=1}^nw_ip(\mu_i)
\quad (\deg p\le2n-1),\qquad
w_i=\frac{2}{(1-\mu_i^2)[P_n'(\mu_i)]^2},\quad \sum_iw_i=2.
\tag{M9.2}
\]
The explicit weight formula is the NIST Gauss-Legendre formula (NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, n.d.).


Proof of Result M9.6
Here \(\deg p\) is polynomial degree. To prove the exactness, divide any polynomial of degree at most \(2n-1\) as \(p=P_ns+r\), with \(s,r\) of degree at most \(n-1\). Orthogonality gives \(\int P_ns=0\), and \(p(\mu_i)=r(\mu_i)\). Integrating the degree-\((n-1)\) Lagrange interpolant of \(r\) exactly therefore integrates \(p\). The Lagrange function that is one at \(\mu_i\) and zero at the other nodes is \(\ell_i(\mu)=P_n(\mu)/[(\mu-\mu_i)P_n'(\mu_i)]\); hence \(w_i=\int\ell_i\). Evaluating this integral with the Legendre recurrence yields the explicit weight formula in (M9.2), specified by the NIST Gauss-Legendre rule. This argument explains the extra exact degrees without assuming uniform latitude spacing. \(\square\)


Definition M9.7 - Full Gaussian grid
A full Gaussian grid combines latitudes \(\varphi_i=\arcsin\mu_i\) with \(M\) equally spaced longitudes \(\lambda_j=2\pi j/M\). No latitude node is at a pole.


Result M9.8 - Quadrature for the area integral and mean
On this full grid, applying the longitude trapezoidal rule and the Gaussian latitude rule gives
\[
\int_{S^2}f\,d\Omega\approx\frac{2\pi}{M}\sum_{i,j}w_if_{ij},
\qquad \langle f\rangle_A\approx\frac1{2M}\sum_{i,j}w_if_{ij}.
\tag{M9.3}
\]
The equality is exact for functions in the respective quadrature exactness classes; for general fields it is an approximation.


Proof of Result M9.8
Write the area integral as \(\int_{-1}^1\int_0^{2\pi}f(\mu,\lambda)d\lambda\,d\mu\). Apply the longitude weight \(2\pi/M\) and latitude weights \(w_i\), then divide by the total solid angle \(4\pi\) for the mean. This gives (M9.3); exactness follows whenever both component rules are exact on the integrand. \(\square\)


Example M9.9 - Area weights and their polynomial limit
For a zonal profile the normalized latitude weights are \(w_i/2\). Multiplying by another \(\cos\varphi_i\) would count the area Jacobian twice. With \(n=2\), nodes \(\pm1/\sqrt3\) and weights one give the exact mean \(1/3\) for \(\mu^2\), but \(1/9\) for \(\mu^4\) instead of \(1/5\); degree four exceeds the exactness guarantee.


Exercise M9.2 - Choose a quadrature order
Application. How many Gauss-Legendre nodes suffice to integrate every polynomial of degree \(8\) exactly? Is the two-node rule sufficient for \(\mu^4\)?

section: 9.3 Exact harmonic recovery and nonlinear aliasing
text:
9.3 Exact harmonic recovery and nonlinear aliasing
Recovering a degree-\(L\) field needs fewer nodes than exactly projecting a quadratic product back to that degree. Dealiasing addresses this second requirement. Sources: (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 12.5–12.6, 14.6); the sufficient spherical bounds follow below.

Definition M9.10 - Separated spherical analysis
For a scalar field bandlimited to degree \(L\), longitude analysis forms \(F_m(\mu_i)=M^{-1}\sum_jf_{ij}e^{-im\lambda_j}\). The normalization \(N_{\ell m}\) is defined by (M8.5).


Result M9.11 - Exact recovery of a degree-limited scalar field
For a scalar field bandlimited to degrees through \(L\), exact arithmetic and a full Gaussian grid satisfying the displayed bounds recover its coefficients:
\[
f_\ell^m=2\pi N_{\ell m}\sum_iw_iF_m(\mu_i)P_\ell^m(\mu_i),
\qquad n\ge L+1,\quad M\ge2L+1.
\tag{M9.4}
\]


Proof of Result M9.11
These bounds make (M9.4) exact in exact arithmetic for the stated bandlimited field. Longitude orthogonality eliminates different orders without aliasing. For the same order, the product \(P_\ell^mP_j^m\) is \((1-\mu^2)^m\) times two polynomial derivatives, with total degree at most \(\ell+j\le2L\). Gaussian quadrature therefore integrates it exactly. Individual odd-order functions need not be polynomials; their same-order products are. \(\square\)


Result M9.12 - Exact low-degree projection of a quadratic scalar product
For the product of two scalar fields bandlimited to degree \(L\), sufficient full Gaussian grid bounds for exact projection back through degree \(L\) are
\[
M>3L,\qquad 2n-1\ge3L.
\tag{M9.5}
\]


Proof of Result M9.12
The product of two degree-\(L\) scalar fields can contain degree \(2L\). To compute its coefficients only through degree \(L\), the integrand contains three harmonics. The largest possible longitude frequency in this triple product is \(3L\), so the strict inequality prevents a nonzero multiple of \(M\) from masquerading as zero. After longitude selection, the sum of the three absolute orders is even, because their signed sum is zero. The factors \((1-\mu^2)^{|m|/2}\) therefore combine into an integer power. The surviving latitude integrand is a polynomial of degree at most \(3L\), and (M9.2) applies. This proves exact low-degree projection, not exact recovery of every degree of the product. It is the reason for padding by roughly a factor \(3/2\) relative to the minimal linear-transform grid. Vector derivatives and higher nonlinearities need their own degree analysis. \(\square\)


Example M9.13 - Linear recovery is weaker than nonlinear projection
For \(L=2\), linear recovery needs \(n\ge3\), \(M\ge5\); quadratic projection needs \(n\ge4\), \(M\ge7\). A solver may use larger integer-friendly sizes. A Fourier example makes the danger explicit: on eight longitude points, multiplying mode \(3\) by mode \(3\) produces mode \(6\), which aliases to \(-2\). Truncating after this aliased transform cannot identify which \(-2\) contribution was physical. Filtering damps modes; dealiasing prevents an incorrect projection. They are different operations.


Exercise M9.3 - A strict longitude bound
Application and boundary case. At \(L=4\), give sufficient \(n,M\) for quadratic projection. Why is \(M=12\) excluded by (M9.5)?

title: 9  Spectral discretization, quadrature, and stability
text:
9.4 Time stepping and numerical stability
Exact spatial modes do not guarantee stable time stepping. Each modal growth factor must fit the time integrator’s stability region. Source: (Arfken and Weber 2005, sec. 9.8, modal diffusion); the discrete amplification calculation is given here explicitly.

Definition M9.14 - Forward-Euler modal amplification
For \(a'=-\gamma a\) with \(\gamma\ge0\), forward Euler with step \(\Delta t>0\) gives \(a^{r+1}=(1-\gamma\Delta t)a^r\), where \(r\) is the integer time index.


Result M9.15 - Forward-Euler bound for spherical diffusion
For \(a\prime=-\gamma a\), \(\gamma\ge0\), forward Euler is nonamplifying if \(0\le\gamma\Delta t\le2\). For spherical diffusion through degree \(L\ge1\),
\[
\gamma_\ell=\frac{\kappa\ell(\ell+1)}{R^2},
\qquad \Delta t\le\frac{2R^2}{\kappa L(L+1)}.
\tag{M9.6}
\]


Proof of Result M9.15
The amplification factor is \(1-\gamma\Delta t\). Requiring its absolute value to be at most one gives the scalar interval. The largest spherical diffusive rate occurs at degree \(L\), so apply the interval to \(\gamma_L=\kappa L(L+1)/R^2\). \(\square\)


Counterexample M9.16 - A small Euler step does not stabilize pure advection
For pure advection \(a'=-i\omega a\) with real nonzero \(\omega\), forward Euler instead has squared amplification \(|1-i\omega\Delta t|^2=1+\omega^2\Delta t^2>1\). A small step reduces growth but does not make this scheme linearly stable for these modes. Backward Euler uses \(a^{r+1}=a^r/(1+\gamma\Delta t)\) for diffusion and is stable for every positive step, while remaining inaccurate for unresolved decay times. An exact exponential update solves a constant linear modal term exactly; forcing and nonlinear coupling still require time approximation.


Definition M9.17 - Courant number, consistency, stability, and convergence
The Courant number \(C=U\Delta t/\Delta x\) compares motion in one step with a grid spacing. A Courant bound is scheme-dependent, not a universal theorem that \(C\le1\) suffices for every method. Consistency means local discretization error vanishes as resolution increases; stability controls error amplification; convergence means the numerical solution approaches the desired continuum solution. Each is a separate claim.


Exercise M9.4 - Separate stability from accuracy
Calculation and interpretation. For \(a\prime=-\gamma a\), compare backward Euler amplification at \(\gamma\Delta t=10\) with exact amplification. Is its magnitude bounded by one?

text:
9.5 Weighted errors and verification
A numerical norm approximates a specified continuum norm. Coordinates and weights belong to the scientific definition of an error. Sources: (Arfken and Weber 2005, secs. 10.3–10.4, 12.3); formulas follow from (M9.3).

Definition M9.18 - Gaussian-weighted error measures
Let \(a_i=w_i/2\) for a zonal profile, truth \(y_i\), prediction \(\widehat y_i\), and error \(e_i=\widehat y_i-y_i\). Then
\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_A=\left(\sum_ia_ie_i^2\right)^{1/2},
\qquad \operatorname{rel}L_A^2=\frac{(\sum_ia_ie_i^2)^{1/2}}{(\sum_ia_iy_i^2)^{1/2}}.
\tag{M9.7}
\]


Remark M9.19 - Units, zero targets, and multiple variables
RMSE means root-mean-square error and has the field’s units; relative \(L^2\) is dimensionless and undefined for zero-norm truth. An arbitrary positive denominator floor defines a different score. For a full field use weights \(w_i/(2M)\). Errors of variables with different units need separate reporting or explicit scales before aggregation.


Remark M9.20 - A verification sequence with distinct failure modes
Useful independent checks are a constant’s area, one harmonic’s coefficients, a transform round trip, discrete Parseval, and an analytic diffusion mode. The first two test normalization and phase; the round trip alone does not test continuous sampling. Convergence studies vary retained degree, quadrature density, and time step separately. Reversing latitude requires reversing both data and weights; a changed longitude origin changes Fourier phases.


Exercise M9.5 - Check the zero predictor
Boundary case. For nonzero-norm truth, what is weighted relative \(L^2\) error of a zero prediction? What if truth also vanishes?

9.6 Chapter summary
Galerkin methods enforce residual orthogonality. Gaussian quadrature uses Legendre roots and integrates through degree \(2n-1\). Spherical integration weights already include the latitude Jacobian. Linear transform recovery needs (M9.4), while exact scalar quadratic projection needs (M9.5). Aliasing, filtering, and truncation are distinct. Modal amplification yields the diffusion time-step bound (M9.6). Weighted errors approximate a chosen physical-area norm.

Independent proof. On a closed sphere let a prescribed smooth tangent velocity be divergence-free, and take \(q_t=-\mathbf u\cdot\nabla_sq\). An exact Galerkin approximation retains the constant harmonic. Prove that its mean coefficient stays constant. Which step would require a new check with approximate quadrature?

title: 10  Kinematics and mathematical language
text:
10.1 Fields, parcels, and the material derivative
Teaching objects and equations prefixed P retain the companion physical-prerequisites numbering. Mathematical operators are introduced in vector calculus and integral theorems. Parcel derivatives and transport are developed in fluid kinematics.
How can Newton’s law describe a fluid when different parcels continually pass the same point? The first task is to distinguish a field from a moving parcel. We then derive the derivative and transport rules that turn conservation of a material quantity into a local field equation.
A derivative at a fixed location differs from the rate experienced by a moving fluid parcel by an advection term. This distinction turns Newton’s law into a field equation. (Vallis 2006, secs. 1.1–1.2)

title: 10  Kinematics and mathematical language
text:
Model P1.1 - Continuum fields and material parcels
A continuum replaces molecular positions with smoothly varying averages on scales large compared with molecular spacing. Let \(\mathbf{x}=(x,y,z)\) be Cartesian position, \(t\) time, and \(\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)\) the velocity field, with units \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). A parcel is a small collection of fluid that moves with the velocity. Its trajectory \(\mathbf{X}(t)\) satisfies \(d\mathbf{X}/dt=\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{X}(t),t)\). The Eulerian description uses fields at fixed \(\mathbf{x}\); the Lagrangian description follows \(\mathbf{X}(t)\).


Definition P1.2 - Material rate of change
For a differentiable scalar field \(b(\mathbf{x},t)\), its material derivative \(Db/Dt\) is the derivative of \(b(\mathbf{X}(t),t)\) along a parcel trajectory. The local derivative \(\partial_t b\) instead holds position fixed.


Result P1.3 - Eulerian formula for the material derivative
For a differentiable field and a parcel moving with \(d\mathbf{X}/dt=\mathbf{v}\), the two rates are related by
 \[
\frac{Db}{Dt}=\partial_t b+\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla b.
\tag{P1.1}
\]


Proof of Result P1.3
For a scalar field \(b(\mathbf{x},t)\), the chain rule gives
\[
\frac{d}{dt}b(\mathbf{X}(t),t)
=\frac{\partial b}{\partial t}
+\frac{dX_x}{dt}\frac{\partial b}{\partial x}
+\frac{dX_y}{dt}\frac{\partial b}{\partial y}
+\frac{dX_z}{dt}\frac{\partial b}{\partial z}.
\]
Here \(\partial_t\) means the partial derivative with respect to time; \(\nabla\) is the spatial gradient introduced in vector calculus. The term \(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla b\) is advection, the change caused by transport through a spatial gradient. In Cartesian components, \(D\mathbf{v}/Dt=\partial_t\mathbf{v}+(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{v}\) is parcel acceleration. A steady field (\(\partial_t b=0\)) need not be materially constant (\(Db/Dt=0\)). \(\square\)


Example P1.4 - A steady field can change along a trajectory
Take \(b=b_0+Gx\) and a uniform velocity \(\mathbf{v}=U\hat{\mathbf{x}}\). Here \(b_0\) is a constant, \(G\) a constant spatial gradient, \(U\) a speed, and \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) the eastward Cartesian unit vector. Then \(\partial_t b=0\), but \(Db/Dt=UG\). This will matter when a parcel moves across latitude-dependent planetary vorticity.

title: 10  Kinematics and mathematical language
text:
10.2 Vector identities used below
Product identities separate flux, advection, and rotation. The book develops the general operators in vector calculus and integral theorems.

Result P1.8 - Product and rotation identities
For smooth scalar \(b\) and vector fields \(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{v}\), mixed derivatives commute, so \(\nabla\times\nabla b=0\) and \(\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{a})=0\). The product identities needed below are
 \[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla\cdot(b\mathbf{a})&=\mathbf{a}\cdot\nabla b+b\nabla\cdot\mathbf{a},\\
(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{v}
&=\nabla\left(\tfrac12|\mathbf{v}|^2\right)
-\mathbf{v}\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{v}).
\end{aligned}\tag{P1.3}
\]


Proof of Result P1.8
Both follow by expanding Cartesian components. The second separates acceleration into a gradient and a rotational contribution. For example, the first identity follows by summing the Cartesian product rules \(\partial_i(ba_i)=a_i\partial_i b+b\partial_i a_i\) over the three directions. \(\square\)

title: 10  Kinematics and mathematical language
text:
10.3 Material volumes and transport
The integral of a field over a moving volume changes both because the field changes and because the volume expands. This is the bridge from parcel conservation to local balance laws. (Vallis 2006, sec. 1.2)

Result P1.9 - Transport through a material volume
Let \(b\) be a smooth density per unit volume and \(V(t)\) a smooth volume transported by \(\mathbf{v}\). Its integral obeys
 \[
\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V(t)}b\,dV
=\int_{V(t)}\left(\frac{Db}{Dt}+b\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}\right)dV
=\int_{V(t)}\left(\partial_tb+\nabla\cdot(b\mathbf{v})\right)dV.
\tag{P1.4}
\]


Derivation of Result P1.9
Track both the value of \(b\) and the volume carrying it. Let \(V(t)\) move with the fluid. An infinitesimal material volume \(\delta V\) changes at the rate \(D\delta V/Dt=(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v})\delta V\): differences between velocities on opposite faces give the three normal expansion rates in the divergence definition. Summing the resulting product rule over all material elements gives (P1.4). The last equality uses the divergence product identity.


Remark P1.10 - Volume and surface area preservation
Here \(b\) is a density per unit volume of whatever is being integrated. It need not be mass density. For a material area \(A(t)\) transported by a tangent velocity \(\mathbf{u}\) on a surface, the analogous area change is \(D\delta A/Dt=(\nabla_h\cdot\mathbf{u})\delta A\). The subscript \(h\) denotes operators within the horizontal surface. Thus non-divergent surface motion preserves area.

title: 10  Kinematics and mathematical language
text:
10.4 Chapter summary

A field is an Eulerian quantity; a trajectory follows a Lagrangian parcel. Parcel acceleration is \(\partial_t\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{v}\).
The material derivative (P1.1) combines local change and advection.
Gradient, divergence, curl, and Laplacian are defined in the vector-calculus chapter. Divergence and Stokes theorems connect local derivatives with flux and circulation.
The transport theorem (P1.4) includes material volume expansion. Non-divergent motion preserves the relevant volume or area.

title: 10  Kinematics and mathematical language
text:
10.5 Exercises

10.5.1 Parcels and fields

Exercise P1.1 - A steady gradient (straightforward)

title: 11  Mass, forces, and the momentum equation
text:
11.1 Mass conservation and incompressibility
Teaching objects and equations prefixed P retain the companion physical-prerequisites numbering. Mathematical operators are introduced in vector calculus and integral theorems. Parcel derivatives and transport are developed in fluid kinematics.
Which forces change parcel momentum, and what does incompressibility actually constrain? We derive the local mass and momentum balances from material conservation laws. The resulting pressure and kinetic-energy equations will separate constraint forces from dissipative forces.
Conservation of parcel mass gives the continuity equation. Incompressibility constrains volume change; it does not by itself make density spatially uniform. (Vallis 2006, secs. 1.2, 1.9)
crumbs: 11  Mass, forces, and the momentum equation

title: 11  Mass, forces, and the momentum equation
text:
Definition P2.1 - Mass density
Mass density \(\rho(\mathbf{x},t)>0\) is mass per unit volume, measured in \(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\). The mass in a material volume is \(\int_{V(t)}\rho\,dV\).


Law P2.2 - Conservation of material mass
In the absence of mass sources, \(d[\int_{V(t)}\rho\,dV]/dt=0\) for every material volume \(V(t)\).


Result P2.3 - Continuity equation
For smooth positive density and velocity satisfying material mass conservation,
 \[
\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf{v})=0,
\qquad \frac{D\rho}{Dt}=-\rho\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}.
\tag{P2.1}
\]


Derivation of Result P2.3
Set \(b=\rho\) in (P1.4). The integral of \(\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf{v})\) is zero over every material volume, so its continuous integrand is zero at each point. Expanding the divergence gives the material form in (P2.1).


Definition P2.4 - Incompressible flow and homogeneous density
An incompressible flow preserves parcel volume: \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}=0\). Then \(D\rho/Dt=0\), although different parcels can retain different densities. A homogeneous fluid has spatially uniform density. The constant-density, incompressible model uses one fixed density \(\rho_0\). These distinctions prevent the incorrect inference that incompressibility alone removes buoyancy (acceleration due to density contrasts in gravity) or density gradients.


Remark P2.5 - Horizontal and three-dimensional divergence differ
Three-dimensional incompressibility gives \(\partial_xu+\partial_yv=-\partial_zw\), where \((u,v,w)\) are velocity components. Thus horizontal divergence need not vanish in an incompressible three-dimensional fluid. The later BVE imposes the stronger, separate restriction \(\nabla_h\cdot\mathbf{u}=0\) on the horizontal velocity \(\mathbf{u}=(u,v)\).


Example P2.6 - An incompressible flow with horizontal convergence
On a local Cartesian domain, let \(u=-cx\), \(v=0\), and \(w=cz\), where \(c>0\) is a constant rate (\(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\)). Then \(\partial_xu+\partial_yv+\partial_zw=-c+0+c=0\), while horizontal divergence is \(-c\). A parcel contracts horizontally and extends vertically without changing volume. The two-dimensional non-divergence restriction used later therefore adds information to three-dimensional incompressibility.

title: 11  Mass, forces, and the momentum equation
text:
11.2 Pressure, stress, and body forces
Newton’s law balances parcel acceleration against pressure forces, viscous stress, and body forces. The constant-viscosity Laplacian is a special case of the stress divergence. (Vallis 2006, sec. 1.3)

Definition P2.7 - Pressure, stress, and body acceleration
Pressure \(p\) is the compressive normal force per unit area (\(\mathrm{Pa}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\)). A surface with outward normal \(\mathbf{n}\) experiences traction \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf{n}\), where the stress tensor \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\) maps a surface orientation to force per area. Write \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}=-p\mathbf{I}+\boldsymbol{\tau}\), where \(\mathbf{I}\) is the identity tensor and \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) the viscous stress. Let \(\mathbf{b}\) be body force per unit mass (\(\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)), such as gravity.


Law P2.8 - Newton’s second law for a material volume
In an inertial frame, Newton’s law on a material volume is
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V(t)}\rho\mathbf{v}\,dV
=\int_{\partial V(t)}\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf{n}\,dA
+\int_{V(t)}\rho\mathbf{b}\,dV.
\]


Result P2.9 - Local momentum balance
For smooth density, velocity, and stress satisfying material mass conservation and Newton’s law, the local momentum equation is
 \[
\rho\frac{D\mathbf{v}}{Dt}=-\nabla p+\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau}+\rho\mathbf{b}.
\tag{P2.2}
\]


Derivation of Result P2.9
Apply (P1.4), cancel terms using (P2.1), and apply the divergence theorem component by component to the stress. Because the volume is arbitrary, the integrands agree pointwise, giving (P2.2).
In Cartesian components, \((\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau})_i=\sum_j\partial_j\tau_{ij}\). The indices \(i,j\) run over three coordinate directions. Every term has units of force per volume. Pressure accelerates fluid toward lower pressure; a uniform pressure has no bulk acceleration because forces on opposite faces cancel.


Model P2.10 - Constant-density Newtonian fluid
For a constant-density, incompressible Newtonian fluid with constant dynamic viscosity \(\mu\geq0\) (\(\mathrm{Pa\,s}\)), the viscous force density is \(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau}=\mu\nabla^2\mathbf{v}\). Newtonian means local viscous shear stress is proportional to local shear rate. This is a constitutive assumption about the material, not a consequence of Newton’s second law. We use the constant-density viscosity model of Vallis, sec. 1.3.3; a general compressible stress law requires additional terms. With \(\nu=\mu/\rho_0\) the kinematic viscosity (\(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\)), (P2.2) becomes the incompressible Navier-Stokes equation
 \[
\frac{D\mathbf{v}}{Dt}=-\frac{1}{\rho_0}\nabla p+\nu\nabla^2\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{b},
\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}=0.
\tag{P2.3}
\]


Definition P2.11 - Euler dynamics and conservative body forces
Dropping viscous stress gives the Euler equation. A force is conservative if it is minus a potential gradient: \(\mathbf{b}=-\nabla\Phi\), where \(\Phi\) has units \(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}\). Its curl vanishes. This property, rather than the mere absence of friction, is needed for circulation conservation.

title: 11  Mass, forces, and the momentum equation
text:
11.3 Pressure closure and kinetic energy
Incompressible pressure enforces the divergence constraint. Viscosity dissipates kinetic energy, whereas pressure redistributes it in a closed constant-density domain. (Vallis 2006, secs. 1.4, 1.10)

Result P2.12 - Pressure as an incompressibility constraint
In the unrotating, constant-density system (P2.3), with constant viscosity, \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}=0\), and conservative body acceleration, define \(\Pi=p/\rho_0+\Phi\). Then pressure is constrained by
\[
\nabla^2\Pi=-\nabla\cdot[(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{v}].
\]


Derivation of Result P2.12
Take the divergence of (P2.3). Time differentiation and the Laplacian commute with divergence, so \(\nabla\cdot\partial_t\mathbf{v}=0\) and \(\nabla\cdot\nabla^2\mathbf{v}=0\). The remaining terms give the displayed Poisson equation, supplemented by the physical boundary conditions.


Remark P2.13 - Diagnostic pressure and thermodynamic closure
Thus pressure is determined diagnostically by an elliptic equation: a spatial boundary-value problem, here a Poisson equation, solved across the domain at each time, rather than independently stepped in time. An additive spatial constant in pressure does not affect motion. This closure is specific to the incompressible reduction. A compressible atmosphere instead also needs an equation of state and a thermodynamic evolution law. For example \(p=\rho R T\) relates ideal-gas pressure, absolute temperature \(T\), and specific gas constant \(R\); it is not by itself a complete evolution system. The constant-density BVE does not retain that thermodynamic system.


Definition P2.14 - Kinetic energy per unit mass
Let \(K=|\mathbf{v}|^2/2\), with units \(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}\).


Result P2.15 - Viscous kinetic-energy sink
For the preceding constant-density system on a periodic volume with no external energy input, \(\nu\geq0\) implies
 \[
\frac{d}{dt}\int_V K\,dV
=-\nu\int_V\sum_{i,j}(\partial_jv_i)^2\,dV\leq0.
\tag{P2.4}
\]


Derivation of Result P2.15
Dot (P2.3) with \(\mathbf{v}\). Use \(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla\Pi=\nabla\cdot(\Pi\mathbf{v})\) and \(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla^2\mathbf{v}=\nabla^2K-\sum_{i,j}(\partial_jv_i)^2\). Integrating over the periodic volume gives (P2.4).
Flux terms integrate to zero by periodicity. The same conclusion holds with suitable stationary no-slip walls. Locally, pressure can do work; its net contribution vanishes under these boundary conditions. Molecular viscosity removes kinetic energy into internal energy; neglecting heat in the reduced equations does not change the sign of this kinetic-energy sink.

title: 11  Mass, forces, and the momentum equation
text:
11.4 Chapter summary

Density \(\rho\), pressure \(p\), stress \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\), and body acceleration \(\mathbf{b}\) enter mass conservation (P2.1) and momentum conservation (P2.2).
Incompressibility means volume preservation; homogeneity means spatially uniform density. Horizontal non-divergence is an additional restriction.
The viscous term \(\nu\nabla^2\mathbf{v}\) requires constant viscosity and incompressibility. The inviscid counterpart is Euler’s equation.
Incompressible pressure enforces the velocity constraint. Conservative forces are potential gradients. Viscosity is a kinetic-energy sink under the stated boundary conditions.

title: 12  Rotation and large-scale balances
text:
12.1 Transforming Newton’s law to a rotating frame
Teaching objects and equations prefixed P retain the companion physical-prerequisites numbering. Mathematical operators are introduced in vector calculus and integral theorems. Parcel derivatives and transport are developed in fluid kinematics.
How does a rotating observer change the equations, and which balances describe large-scale motion? We derive the inertial-to-rotating transformation before making local-plane or balance approximations. This keeps exact frame effects separate from hydrostatic, geostrophic, and single-layer assumptions.
Uniform rotation adds Coriolis and centrifugal accelerations. Coriolis changes velocity direction without doing work. (Vallis 2006, secs. 2.1–2.2)

title: 12  Rotation and large-scale balances
text:
Assumption P3.1 - Uniformly rotating reference frame
Let \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) be the constant angular velocity of the reference frame, \(\Omega=|\boldsymbol{\Omega}|\), and \(\mathbf{r}\) position relative to its fixed origin. Let subscripts \(I\) and \(R\) denote inertial and rotating observers. Rotating basis vectors obey \(d\hat{\mathbf{e}}/dt=\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\hat{\mathbf{e}}\). We differentiate vectors in these two frames by differentiating their components and their basis vectors.


Result P3.2 - Velocity and acceleration transformation
For a fixed origin and constant frame angular velocity \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\), the inertial and rotating velocities and accelerations satisfy
 \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{v}_I&=\mathbf{v}_R+\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{r},\\
\mathbf{a}_I&=\frac{D\mathbf{v}_R}{Dt}
+2\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{v}_R
+\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{r}).
\end{aligned}\tag{P3.1}
\]


Derivation of Result P3.2
Differentiate both vector components and their rotating basis. The basis-vector relation above gives
\[
\left(\frac{d\mathbf{a}}{dt}\right)_I
=\left(\frac{d\mathbf{a}}{dt}\right)_R+\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{a}.
\]
Apply this to \(\mathbf{r}\) and then its velocity: Because \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) is constant, applying this rule twice gives (P3.1), with two equal cross terms that produce the factor 2.


Definition P3.3 - Effective geopotential
There is no angular-acceleration term because \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) is constant. From now on \(\mathbf{v}\) means velocity relative to the rotating frame. With gravitational potential \(\Phi_g\), define the effective geopotential \(\Phi=\Phi_g-|\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{r}|^2/2\). Indeed \(\nabla(|\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{r}|^2/2)=-\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{r})\), so centrifugal acceleration is included in \(-\nabla\Phi\). This definition absorbs centrifugal acceleration into a conservative body-force potential.


Result P3.4 - Momentum in the rotating frame
Let \(\mathbf{F}\) collect non-conservative acceleration, including viscosity if retained. Expressing the local momentum balance in this uniformly rotating frame gives
 \[
\frac{D\mathbf{v}}{Dt}+2\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{v}
=-\frac{1}{\rho}\nabla p-\nabla\Phi+\mathbf{F}.
\tag{P3.2}
\]


Derivation of Result P3.4
Substitute (P3.1) for inertial acceleration, transfer the Coriolis term to the left, and absorb the centrifugal term in the effective geopotential. Here \(\mathbf{F}\) collects non-conservative accelerations, including viscosity if retained. Coriolis acceleration on the right-hand side is \(-2\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{v}\). Because \(\mathbf{v}\cdot(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\times\mathbf{v})=0\), it contributes no kinetic-energy work. Rotation nevertheless changes which velocity fields solve the equation.

title: 12  Rotation and large-scale balances
section: 12.2 The Coriolis parameter and local planes
text:
12.2 The Coriolis parameter and local planes
The radial projection of planetary vorticity varies with latitude. Its northward gradient provides the restoring mechanism of Rossby waves. (Vallis 2006, sec. 2.3)

Definition P3.5 - Radial planetary vorticity
Let \(a\) be planetary radius, \(\phi\) latitude, \(\lambda\) longitude, and \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\) the local outward radial unit vector. Define \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\lambda\) eastward and \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\phi\) northward; \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\lambda\times\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\phi=\hat{\mathbf{k}}\). The Coriolis parameter is
 \[
f=2\boldsymbol{\Omega}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{k}}=2\Omega\sin\phi.
\tag{P3.3}
\]


Model P3.6 - Traditional rotation approximation
It has units \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Retaining only this component of rotation in horizontal momentum is the traditional approximation. For horizontal speed \(U\) and vertical speed magnitude \(|w|\), the neglected horizontal coupling is small relative to \(|f|U\) when \((|w|/U)|\cot\phi|\ll1\). Neglecting the corresponding vertical Coriolis contribution also requires a consistent vertical momentum scaling, such as the shallow, stratified large-scale regime discussed by Vallis. It is an approximation, not a statement that the full rotation vector is vertical. On a strictly two-dimensional constrained spherical shell, the tangent Coriolis acceleration from tangent velocity is exactly \(-f\hat{\mathbf{k}}\times\mathbf{u}\).


Model P3.7 - Local tangent-plane coordinates
In a small neighborhood of latitude \(\phi_0\), let \(x=a\cos\phi_0(\lambda-\lambda_0)\) and \(y=a(\phi-\phi_0)\) be local eastward and northward distances; \(\lambda_0\) is a reference longitude. The local planetary-vorticity expansion follows from these coordinates.


Result P3.8 - Local planetary-vorticity gradient
For meridional distances small compared with \(a\), Taylor expansion at \(\phi_0\) gives
 \[
f=f_0+\beta y+O\!\left(\Omega y^2/a^2\right),\quad
f_0=2\Omega\sin\phi_0,\quad
\beta=\frac{2\Omega\cos\phi_0}{a}.
\tag{P3.4}
\]


Derivation of Result P3.8
Insert \(\phi=\phi_0+y/a\) in \(f=2\Omega\sin\phi\) and retain the constant and linear terms. The linear coefficient is \(df/dy=(2\Omega/a)\cos\phi_0\); the next term has scale \(\Omega y^2/a^2\).


Definition P3.9 - \(f\)-plane and \(\beta\)-plane
\(O(\cdot)\) denotes the scale of omitted terms. An \(f\)-plane uses constant \(f_0\); a \(\beta\)-plane retains \(\beta y\) but otherwise uses flat geometry. Here \(\beta\) has units \(\mathrm{m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\). This expansion needs distances small compared with \(a\). The sphere later retains the full sine and metric factors. A constant-\(f\) homogeneous layer has no planetary-vorticity-gradient Rossby waves, although other potential-vorticity gradients can support analogous waves.


Example P3.10 - Coriolis deflection without work
On an \(f\)-plane with no horizontal pressure gradient or friction, take \(u(0)=U>0\) and \(v(0)=0\). The momentum components are \(\dot u=f_0v\) and \(\dot v=-f_0u\). Direct differentiation verifies \(u=U\cos(f_0t)\) and \(v=-U\sin(f_0t)\), with \(u^2+v^2=U^2\). Thus an initially eastward velocity turns southward when \(f_0>0\), while its speed stays fixed. This motion is an inertial oscillation, with period \(2\pi/|f_0|\) for \(f_0\ne0\).

title: 12  Rotation and large-scale balances
text:
12.3 Scaling, hydrostatic balance, and geostrophy
Small aspect ratio and small Rossby number justify useful leading balances, but neither alone derives the non-divergent BVE. (Vallis 2006, secs. 1.11, 2.7–2.8)

Definition P3.11 - Aspect ratio, Rossby number, and Reynolds number
Choose positive representative horizontal speed \(U\), horizontal length \(L\), depth \(H\), and advective time \(L/U\). The aspect ratio is \(H/L\). The Rossby number and Reynolds number are
 \[
\mathrm{Ro}=\frac{U}{|f_0|L},\qquad
\mathrm{Re}=\frac{UL}{\nu}.
\tag{P3.5}
\]
For \(f_0\ne0\) and \(\nu>0\), they compare advective acceleration with Coriolis acceleration, and advection with molecular viscosity. The inviscid limit corresponds to \(\mathrm{Re}\to\infty\). Both are dimensionless. If the evolution time differs substantially from \(L/U\), also compare its inverse with \(|f_0|\). Large \(\mathrm{Re}\) does not mean all dissipation can be omitted at unresolved small scales. Small \(\mathrm{Ro}\) is not required by the full BVE; it is used for geostrophic interpretation. Formula (P3.5) does not define a useful geostrophic ordering at \(f_0=0\).


Model P3.12 - Hydrostatic balance and its scaling limits
For incompressible large-scale flow, continuity suggests vertical speed of order \(UH/L\). Vertical acceleration then scales as \(U^2H/L^2\). A hydrostatic approximation drops this acceleration relative to the vertical pressure and gravity balance:
 \[
\partial_zp=-\rho g,
\tag{P3.6}
\]
where \(z\) increases upward and \(g>0\) is effective gravitational acceleration. A necessary smallness estimate is \(U^2H/(gL^2)\ll1\); accurate horizontal pressure gradients can require a stronger ordering based on pressure departures and stratification, as emphasized by Vallis, sec. 2.7. Hydrostatic balance does not set vertical velocity to zero and does not remove horizontal density variation.


Model P3.13 - Geostrophic leading balance
For constant reference density \(\rho_0\) and \(\mathrm{Ro}\ll1\), the leading horizontal balance on an \(f\)-plane is geostrophy:
 \[
f_0\hat{\mathbf{k}}\times\mathbf{u}_g=-\frac{1}{\rho_0}\nabla_hp,
\qquad
u_g=-\frac{1}{\rho_0f_0}\partial_yp,\quad
v_g=\frac{1}{\rho_0f_0}\partial_xp.
\tag{P3.7}
\]
Here \(\mathbf{u}_g=(u_g,v_g)\) is geostrophic velocity. Opposing pressure-gradient and Coriolis forces give flow along pressure contours, rather than direct flow toward low pressure. Defining \(\psi_g=p/(\rho_0f_0)\) gives \(\mathbf{u}_g=\hat{\mathbf{k}}\times\nabla_h\psi_g\). Its divergence vanishes for constant \(f_0\). With latitude-dependent \(f\), this pressure-based velocity is not exactly non-divergent. The BVE streamfunction below is defined kinematically, without imposing geostrophy.

title: 12  Rotation and large-scale balances
section: 12.4 Barotropic density and the role of stratification
text:
12.4 Barotropic density and the role of stratification
A barotropic equation of state eliminates baroclinic vorticity production; a one-layer, depth-independent velocity is a further modeling restriction. This distinction explains what stochastic stirring replaces. (Vallis 2006, secs. 2.4, 2.8–2.9, 4.2)

Definition P3.14 - Barotropic and baroclinic density-pressure structure
A barotropic fluid satisfies \(p=p(\rho)\), or locally \(\rho=\rho(p)\) where invertible. Pressure and density gradients are parallel, so \(\nabla\rho\times\nabla p=0\). Baroclinicity means these gradients are not parallel. A constant-density fluid also makes this cross product zero. The thermodynamic definition alone does not force every possible velocity field to be independent of height.


Model P3.15 - Boussinesq balanced density departures
To see the connection under balanced conditions, use a local Boussinesq model: density departures \(\rho'\) from constant \(\rho_0\) are retained in the vertical buoyancy acceleration \(b=-g\rho'/\rho_0\) but omitted from inertia. Buoyancy is the acceleration caused by a parcel’s density difference from its hydrostatic surroundings; a denser parcel has \(b<0\). Let \(p'\) be pressure relative to a hydrostatic reference state. Combine \(f_0\hat{\mathbf{k}}\times\mathbf{u}_g=-\nabla_hp'/\rho_0\) with \(\partial_zp'=-g\rho'\).


Result P3.16 - Thermal-wind relation
For constant \(f_0\ne0\) and \(\rho_0\), if geostrophic and hydrostatic perturbation balances hold in the stated Boussinesq model, then
 \[
f_0\hat{\mathbf{k}}\times\partial_z\mathbf{u}_g
=\frac{g}{\rho_0}\nabla_h\rho'.
\tag{P3.8}
\]


Derivation of Result P3.16
Differentiate \(f_0\hat{\mathbf{k}}\times\mathbf{u}_g=-\nabla_hp'/\rho_0\) with respect to height. Commuting \(\partial_z\) with \(\nabla_h\) and inserting \(\partial_zp'=-g\rho'\) gives (P3.8).


Remark P3.17 - What thermal wind does and does not imply
It relates vertical shear of geostrophic velocity to horizontal density gradients; it is not an extra wind component. In this approximation, no horizontal density gradient implies no vertical geostrophic shear. Arbitrary unbalanced motions need not obey this inference.


Result P3.18 - Buoyancy frequency in a resting Boussinesq fluid
Consider a density-conserving parcel initially matching its hydrostatic surroundings at reference height \(z_0\). For a small displacement \(\eta\) from that height in the resting Boussinesq reference density \(\bar\rho(z)\), with the gradient evaluated at \(z_0\), acceleration is \(\ddot\eta=-N^2\eta\), with
\[
N^2=-\frac{g}{\rho_0}\frac{d\bar\rho}{dz}.
\]


Derivation of Result P3.18
For a resting Boussinesq reference density \(\bar\rho(z)\), a small upward parcel displacement \(\eta\) leaves the parcel with density excess \(-\eta\,d\bar\rho/dz\). The parcel keeps its initial density while its surroundings change by \(\eta\,d\bar\rho/dz\); the resulting buoyancy acceleration is \(g\eta(d\bar\rho/dz)/\rho_0=-N^2\eta\).


Definition P3.19 - Stable stratification and dry-air potential temperature
\(N\) is the buoyancy frequency when \(N^2>0\): the stratification is stable and resists displacement. Negative \(N^2\) indicates instability in this simple parcel model. For dry ideal-gas air, define potential temperature \(\theta_T=T(p_{\mathrm{ref}}/p)^{R/c_p}\), where \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}>0\) is a fixed reference pressure and \(c_p\) is constant specific heat at constant pressure (\(\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}\)). It is the temperature a parcel would have after compression or expansion to \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}\) without heat exchange; it is conserved in dry reversible adiabatic motion. In compressible air, the corresponding stability criterion uses potential temperature, not the raw vertical density gradient; we do not apply this Boussinesq formula to a compressible atmospheric profile. Stratification and thermal wind allow three-dimensional baroclinic dynamics that a homogeneous single-layer BVE omits. Random stirring can parameterize some eddy input from such omitted motions without reproducing their thermodynamics.

title: 12  Rotation and large-scale balances
text:
12.5 Chapter summary

A rotating frame adds Coriolis acceleration and centrifugal acceleration. The latter enters effective geopotential; Coriolis does no work.
\(f=2\Omega\sin\phi\) is planetary vorticity normal to the surface; \(\beta=2\Omega\cos\phi_0/a\) is its local northward gradient.
Rossby number, Reynolds number, and aspect ratio describe distinct approximations. Hydrostatic balance is vertical; geostrophic balance is horizontal.
Barotropy removes the density-pressure cross product. Thermal wind links balanced vertical shear to horizontal density variation. Stable stratification resists vertical displacement.
The two-dimensional constant-depth BVE requires explicit restrictions beyond hydrostasy, geostrophy, or thermodynamic barotropy.
